paragraphs: To set out the general cause of these differences, we must distinguish here between government and its principle, as we distinguished earlier between the State and the Sovereign.

The body of magistrates may be made up of a greater or smaller number of members. We said that the relation of the Sovereign to the subjects is greater in proportion as the people is more numerous; and, by a clear analogy, we may say the same of the relation of the government to the magistrates.

But the total force of the government is always that of the State, and so it does not vary. The more of this force the government spends on its own members, the less it has left to use on the whole people.
The more magistrates there are, then, the weaker the government. This principle is fundamental, so we must do our best to make it clear.

In the person of the magistrate we can distinguish three essentially different wills. First, the private will of the individual, which tends only to his personal advantage. Second, the common will of the magistrates, which relates solely to the advantage of the prince, and which may be called corporate will; it is general in relation to the government and particular in relation to the State, of which the government forms a part. Third, the will of the people, or the sovereign will, which is general both in relation to the State regarded as the whole and in relation to the government regarded as a part of the whole.

In a perfect act of legislation, the individual or particular will should count for nothing. The corporate will of the government should hold a very minor place. The general or sovereign will should therefore always prevail, and be the sole guide for all the rest.

According to the natural order, on the other hand, these different wills become more active the more they are concentrated. Thus the general will is always the weakest, the corporate will second, and the individual will the strongest of all. So in the government each member is first of all himself, then a magistrate, and then a citizen — in an order exactly the reverse of what the social system requires.

Granting this, suppose the whole government is in the hands of one man. Then the particular will and the corporate will are wholly united, and so the corporate will is at the highest degree of intensity it can reach. But the use made of the force depends on the degree the will reaches, and the absolute force of the government does not vary. It follows that the most active government is that of one man.

Suppose, on the other hand, we unite the government with the legislative authority, make the Sovereign the prince as well, and make all the citizens so many magistrates. Then the corporate will, being merged with the general will, can be no more active than that will, and must leave the particular will as strong as it can possibly be. Thus the government, always having the same absolute force, will be at the lowest point of its relative force or activity.

These relations are beyond dispute, and there are other considerations that confirm them further. We can see, for instance, that each magistrate is more active in the body to which he belongs than each citizen is in the body to which he belongs. Consequently the particular will has much more influence on the acts of the government than on those of the Sovereign; for each magistrate is almost always charged with some function of government, while each citizen, taken singly, exercises no function of Sovereignty. Furthermore, the bigger the State grows, the more its real force increases, though not in direct proportion to its growth. But with the State remaining the same, the number of magistrates may increase to any extent without the government gaining any greater real force; for its force is that of the State, whose size stays the same. Thus the relative force or activity of the government decreases, while its absolute or real force cannot increase.

Moreover, it is certain that promptness in carrying out business diminishes as more people are put in charge of it. Where too much is made of prudence, too little is made of fortune; opportunity is let slip, and deliberation causes the loss of its object.

I have just shown that the government grows slack in proportion as the number of magistrates increases; and I showed earlier that the more numerous the people, the greater the repressive force should be. From this it follows that the relation of the magistrates to the government should vary inversely to the relation of the subjects to the Sovereign. That is to say, the larger the State, the more the government should be tightened, so that the number of rulers diminishes in proportion as the number of the people increases.

I should add that I am speaking here of the government’s relative strength, not of its rectitude. In that respect the reverse holds: the more numerous the magistracy, the closer the corporate will comes to the general will, while under a single magistrate the corporate will is, as I said, merely a particular will. So what is gained on one side is lost on the other. The art of the legislator is to know how to fix the point where the force and the will of the government, which are always in inverse proportion, meet in the relation that serves the State best.
